prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I moved my own first-place candidate, IceCube (B052), below the optical lattice clock after reading the openings. B009 is the only candidate that all eight of us ranked, with three first places and six top-three rankings, and the support rests on scientific arguments rather than habit. It is an instrument invention in the best sense: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping lets many atoms be interrogated at once in a Doppler- and recoil-free regime, and Ye's group drove the strontium clock to about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. That precision opens a new measurement regime for relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, searches for variation of constants and dark-matter signatures, and a redefinition of the second. The credited pair is clean and every colleague who proposed laureates named the same two people. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by independent clocks at RIKEN, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and international clock comparisons agree. As an instrument builder I know how much patient work on systematics lies behind a number like that, and the community believes it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and overlap. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb that makes optical clocks usable, and the 2012 prize covered ion control and ion clocks, so a sceptic can call the lattice clock an incremental step in a line already honoured. There is also a real question of whether Ye's decisive contribution is the clock itself or the broader JILA programme (comb-linked spectroscopy, many-body spin-exchange physics) and whether Hall's earlier role shapes the allocation. Finally, the timing argument depends on the pending redefinition of the second, which has not happened. Atomic physics is outside my own expertise, so I treat these as questions for the expert reviewers and not as settled objections.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a textbook case of a measurement technique that moved the limit of what can be measured, and puts atom interferometry (B001) and optical-lattice quantum simulation (B010) next.
responses.response: I agree with the instrument framing and it is the main reason I now lead with B009. I do not yet share your enthusiasm for atom interferometry as the next candidate. Its most compelling applications, such as field gravimeters and equivalence-principle tests, are still maturing, and the credit is split across Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich in a way that the optical lattice clock does not suffer from. I would keep B001 out of my own configuration for now.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first because many independent laboratories running Sr, Yb and Hg clocks give mutually consistent results, and sees a path to redefining the second.
responses.response: That independent-confirmation point is exactly my test for a lasting result, and it is stronger here than for IceCube, where the sources of most of the flux are still unidentified. I would press you on one thing. The redefinition of the second is a consequence of the invention and not part of the discovery, so I would keep the citation on the clock and its precision and not hang it on the redefinition, which could still be delayed.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B018) first as a genuinely new class of quantum matter, and puts the optical lattice clock only sixth.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual weight of B018, but I disagree on its ordering and on its readiness. Only three members ranked it, and Mehlig points out that the 2016 prize and the unresolved Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit make the allocation messy. Condensed-matter topology is outside my expertise, so I defer to you on the science, but I would ask you to say what the decisive experimental contribution is beyond Molenkamp's HgTe observation. Until that is settled I cannot put B018 ahead of a candidate with a clean attribution and eight-member support.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the CMB anisotropy mapping (B050) first, as a mature field-defining measurement that confirms the standard cosmological model, and puts the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I rank B050 fourth and I agree it is scientifically deep. My difficulty is attribution, which you also flag. The credited set omits Planck leadership and the balloon experiments, WMAP is a large collaboration, and Puget appears in the shortlist names but not in your three. Until that is resolved the CMB cannot beat the lattice clock, which has a clean pair. If the committee wants an astrophysics prize this year I would prefer to settle the IceCube or EHT allocation first, since those are also open.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the lattice clock first as a genuine invention that opened a door, ranks IceCube fifth and the EHT sixth.
responses.response: We agree on B009. On IceCube I would qualify your fifth place: the 2013 diffuse flux, TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 give independent routes to the same conclusion, and KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD support the flux. The weakness is attribution, since Halzen, Karle and Spiering cannot represent the whole collaboration and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers are not credited. That is why I keep it as an alternative and not as the preferred prize.

uncertainties: Whether the overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes weakens the novelty of the lattice clock for the full committee.
Whether Jun Ye's credit is best framed as the strontium clock itself or the wider JILA programme, and whether other lattice-clock groups (for example NIST, PTB, SYRTE) need to be considered.
I rely on colleagues and expert reviewers for atomic physics, and on memory for the detailed history of the IceCube phases if it comes back as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B009. As a PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaboration member and a cosmic-ray and astroparticle specialist, I have a general field closeness to the IceCube candidate (B052), but I name no personal connection to its credited people, and I do not see a need to recuse myself.
